_README: DIVE SITES.
Twenty-two sites, compiled from dive-operator and dive-guide sources and
cross-checked where they overlapped. Names, types and depths are as
published by the operators who run them. Descriptions and tips are ours.
COORDINATES ARE APPROXIMATE, and the first attempt at them was wrong
enough to be worth recording. Sites were dropped at coordinates read off
written descriptions, which put the whole Sandy Bay cluster ON the
village — 40 to 140 metres from a shore business, i.e. inland — and the
West End group 3 km out in open ocean, when that reef is a few hundred
metres off the shore.
They are now constructed rather than guessed. Each cluster has a local
coastal frame built from the app's own business medians: an along-shore
direction and a seaward normal.
west coast   along = West Bay -> West End,      seaward = west
north coast  along = West End -> Sandy Bay,     seaward = NNW
south coast  along = Dixon Cove -> French H.,   seaward = SSE
Every site is then placed as an along-shore offset plus a seaward one, so
it is in the water by construction and sits in its own bay. Offshore
distances follow the site: 220-350 m for a shallow reef or house reef,
400-550 m for a wall, 950 m for Josie J because it bottoms at 65 m and
the drop-off is further out. Everything now lies between 170 m and 2 km
off the nearest shore business, which is the range these sites actually
occupy.
An earlier attempt drew the north coast as one straight line from Sandy
Bay to Palmetto Bay. That chord cuts inland across 10 km of coast, so
sites placed along it landed on the island again. Hence the local frames:
there is no business data on the north coast between those two points to
bend the line with.
This is still orientation, not navigation, and the detail screen says so.
Real GPS from a dive computer or an operator beats all of it.
THREE PLACEMENTS ARE SHAKIER THAN THE REST:
- Dolphin Den. Tagged french_harbour and placed on the south shore to
match, but which coast it is on was never confirmed. If it is a north
shore site, it is in the wrong sea.
- Mary's Place. Moved from Coxen Hole to the south shore near Brick
Bay, on a source that says 'south side, close to Brick Bay'.
- El Aguila. A source puts it 'north side near West End' rather than at
Sandy Bay proper, so it sits at the west end of the Sandy Bay stretch.
TO VERIFY WITH A DIVE MASTER, in priority order:
1. depths and levels — this is safety information
2. operatorSlugs — EMPTY on every site except Front Porch, because we
won't claim a shop runs a site without knowing. Fill these and the
two-way link between sites and shops lights up. Slugs come from
businesses.json: native-sons-diving, coconut-tree-divers,
west-end-divers, sun-divers-roatan, roatan-divers, west-bay-divers,
mayan-divers, paradise-beach-dive-center, anthonys-key-resort.
3. the coordinates above
Any field set to null is simply omitted from the UI — a site with no
recorded depth shows no depth rather than a plausible default. Set
'active': false to hide a site without deleting it.

sites.name: West End Wall
sites.summary: A drift along the edge of the reef where the shelf gives way and the bottom simply disappears. You hang off the wall and let the current do the work. One of the dives people mean when they say they came to Roatán to dive.
sites.insiderTip: Ask to be dropped up-current and drift toward the point — swimming this one is a waste of a tank.

sites.name: Texas
sites.summary: The drift that carries on from West End Wall or Pablo's Place, out where the current runs hardest. Giant barrel sponges and soft coral the whole way, and the moving water is what brings the bigger animals through.
sites.insiderTip: This is the one to ask for when the current is up — most divers avoid it then, which is exactly when it's best.

sites.name: Blue Channel
sites.summary: A cut through the reef with swim-throughs at one end and a shallow sandy bowl at the other that fills with fish. Shallow enough that you get a long dive out of it, varied enough that it never feels like a shallow dive.
sites.insiderTip: Long bottom time here — plan it as your second tank and you'll still be under when everyone else is up.

sites.name: Half Moon Bay Wall
sites.summary: The reef stands up shallow at about thirty feet and then drops away past a hundred and fifty. Healthy hard coral the whole length of it, and close enough to shore that you can reach it without a boat.
sites.insiderTip: One of the few walls here you can swim to from the beach. Go early, before the bay fills with snorkellers.

sites.name: Turtle Crossing
sites.summary: Coral channels between two sandy plateaus, one at twenty feet and one at forty-five, leading out to a wall that drops to a hundred and twenty. The name is not decoration.
sites.insiderTip: Spend the first half on the plateaus rather than rushing the wall — that's where the turtles actually are.

sites.name: Josie J
sites.summary: A wreck sitting at two hundred and thirteen feet just off West End Wall. Beyond recreational limits — this one is for technical divers with the training and the gas to match.

sites.name: Herbie's Fantasy
sites.summary: Also called Tabyana. Shallow coral garden with some of the healthiest hard and soft coral anywhere in the Caribbean, and the colour to prove it. Photographers ask for this one by name.
sites.insiderTip: Bring a macro lens or nothing at all — the seahorses and frogfish here are the point.

sites.name: Seaquest
sites.summary: Sandy patches from twenty to forty feet with the top of the reef sitting shallow, then a steep drop to ninety. A site that works for a first open-water dive and still holds something for a hundredth.

sites.name: El Aguila
sites.summary: A two-hundred-and-thirty-foot freighter sunk deliberately as an artificial reef in 1997, then broken into three pieces by Hurricane Mitch. That's how she still lies, at about a hundred and ten feet, thoroughly grown in.
sites.insiderTip: The green morays living in the wreck are enormous and entirely used to divers. Don't feed them.

sites.name: The Odyssey
sites.summary: Three hundred feet of freighter on a sandy bottom at about a hundred and ten, sunk in 2002 after a fire finished her working life. The biggest wreck on the island and easily a two-dive site.
sites.insiderTip: Too big to see in one tank. Do the bow one dive and the stern the next.

sites.name: Spooky Channel
sites.summary: An ancient waterfall, drowned. The channel starts shallow and drops to ninety feet, about fifty feet across at its widest, and the walls lean in overhead until they're a few feet apart. Very little light reaches the bottom, which is where the name comes from.
sites.insiderTip: Look up, not down. The ribbon of light eighty feet above you is the whole reason to dive it.

sites.name: Front Porch
sites.summary: Anthony's Key's house reef, and an easy shore entry. The kind of site you dive at the end of the day when the boats have finished and you just want to be in the water.

sites.name: Peter's Place
sites.summary: A wall dive just north of the El Aguila, running to about a hundred feet, full of crevices and small canyons. Works as a drift, and you can carry on north to Bear's Den on the same tank.

sites.name: Bear's Den
sites.summary: Opens with a hundred-and-twenty-foot chimney at fifty feet down, which lets you out onto a honeycombed coral wall. Closer to caving than reef diving, and it wants buoyancy you can trust.
sites.insiderTip: Don't go in behind someone who's silting it up. Wait, or lead.

sites.name: Overheat Reef
sites.summary: Named years ago because a dive boat's engine used to overheat at this exact spot. Shallow sandy plateau with soft coral, then a seven-minute swim out to a proper drop-off.
sites.insiderTip: The swim out is where the small stuff is. Don't sprint it to reach the wall.

sites.name: Butcher's Bank
sites.summary: Shallow sand that rewards going slowly, then a coral platform on the way out to the wall. Not a dramatic site, and it doesn't need to be — this is where you find the things that hide.

sites.name: Hole in the Wall
sites.summary: A sand chute leads down to the hole itself at a hundred and thirty feet — about as deep as recreational diving goes here. Beyond it, a network of swim-throughs like swiss cheese and a small cave system.
sites.insiderTip: Watch your gas. It's easy to lose track down the chute and the ascent is long.

sites.name: Calvin's Crack
sites.summary: A narrow entrance you go into head first, dropping through the reef and opening out onto the wall at about ninety feet. Short, memorable, and not for anyone unsure about tight spaces.
sites.insiderTip: Go feet-first back out if the crack is busy — turning around in there is not a plan.

sites.name: Canyon Reef
sites.summary: Canyons, cuts and swim-throughs with the wall bottoming out at about fifty-five feet, which keeps the whole thing inside open-water limits. All the topography of a deep site at a depth anyone can dive.

sites.name: Fish Den
sites.summary: The mooring sits on a coral pillar in a square cut in the reef wall. The top of the pillar is at twenty feet, it drops to forty, and the hole slopes away to sixty.

sites.name: Dolphin Den
sites.summary: An underwater maze of tunnels linking one canyon to the next, at fifty to seventy feet. The navigation is the dive — you surface somewhere quite different from where you dropped.
sites.insiderTip: Stay on your guide's fins. It is genuinely easy to take a wrong turn in here.

sites.name: Mary's Place
sites.summary: The site everyone comes to Roatán for. A plateau at thirty feet where the reef's corner juts out like an elbow and splits away from the rest, opening a fissure that runs down to a hundred and twenty. An old earthquake did it.
sites.insiderTip: Buoyancy matters more here than anywhere on the island — the crack is narrow and the coral on both sides is irreplaceable.
